name: Benchmark Suites
question: How does it compare with the field?
summary: Public benchmark suites measure general agent capability on standard tasks with fixed harnesses. Use them to choose a model or framework. They are no substitute for an eval set built from your own tasks.
useCases: Shortlisting models or frameworks before you build
Tracking general capability across model upgrades
Reporting progress against a shared yardstick

items.detail: 500 human-validated GitHub issues; the patch must pass the repo’s tests
466 real-world assistant questions over 3 difficulty levels
tool use with simulated users in retail and airline domains; reports pass^k
369 computer-use tasks on real desktop apps
Berkeley Function Calling Scoreboard: tool-call accuracy

steps: Pick the suites closest to your agent’s work: code, web, tools or desktop
Run the official harness and settings so results are comparable
Report pass@1, cost and run time, not just the headline score
Mirror the format in a private set built from your own tasks
pitfalls: Contamination: test items may be in the model’s training data
Saturation: top scores stop separating strong systems
Scoreboard setups often differ from your production constraints
remember: Benchmarks to choose, private evals to ship.
caption: Which capabilities each benchmark exercises. Choose the ones that match your agent’s job.

code.text: # Your agent writes one patch per issue:
# Per instance: build Docker env, apply patch, run tests
# FAIL_TO_PASS must now pass; PASS_TO_PASS must still pass
# Report resolved / 500 with cost and run time,
# then rerun the finalists on your own issues.

steps.title: Pick the benchmark
steps.text: Choose the suite closest to your workload. SWE-bench Verified: 500 human-checked GitHub issues from Python repositories.

steps.title: Generate predictions
steps.text: Your agent attempts each issue and writes one patch per instance ID into preds.jsonl.

steps.title: Run the official harness
steps.text: The harness builds a Docker environment per repository and applies each patch, so results are reproducible.

steps.title: Tests decide
steps.text: FAIL_TO_PASS tests must now pass (the issue is fixed) and PASS_TO_PASS tests must still pass (nothing broke).

steps.title: Report, then confirm privately
steps.text: Report the resolved rate with cost and time. Then run the finalists on your own issues before choosing.

playgroundGuide.scenario: You must pick a model for an internal coding assistant. Alpha, Beta and Gamma (fictional) each have a public scoreboard score and a score from your own 60-issue internal eval. See how the choice changes with what you trust and what you optimise.
controls: Scores from: the public scoreboard or your internal eval.
Rank by: resolve rate (quality) or cost per resolved task (efficiency).
Tasks per month: your expected volume.

practice.scenario: Before choosing a model for an internal coding assistant, a team compares published SWE-bench Verified results to shortlist two candidates. It then runs both on 60 closed issues from its own repositories, and that private result, not the scoreboard, decides the pick.

τ-bench mirrors their customer-service tool workflows
OSWorld and WebArena map to desktop and browser back-office automation

practice.analogy: A board-exam rank versus a job interview. The rank shortlists candidates; the interview on your real work decides who you hire.

library.name: SWE-bench harness
library.what: The official Docker-based harness. It applies each patch, runs the repository tests and reports resolved issues.

samples.code:
# preds.jsonl: one JSON line per issue your agent attempted
# {"instance_id": "django__django-11099",
#  "model_name_or_path": "my-agent",
#  "model_patch": "diff --git a/..."}

python -m swebench.harness.run_evaluation \
  --dataset_name princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified \
  --predictions_path preds.jsonl \
  --max_workers 8 \
  --run_id my-agent-v1

# Output: a JSON report with resolved / unresolved instance IDs

numericDrill.question: Model A resolves 62% of SWE-bench Verified at $0.40 per task. Model B resolves 58% at $0.10. Over 1,000 tasks, what is B's cost per resolved issue, in $?
numericDrill.answer: A: $400 ÷ 620 ≈ $0.65 per resolved issue. B: $100 ÷ 580 ≈ $0.17. B is about 4× cheaper per resolved issue for 4 points less.

interview.question: Why can't you choose a model on scoreboard scores alone?
interview.answer: Benchmarks can be contaminated or saturated, run with harness settings unlike yours, and cover different tasks. Use them to shortlist, then decide with a private eval on your own tasks.

interview.question: What does SWE-bench Verified measure?
interview.answer: Whether an agent can resolve real GitHub issues from Python repositories: its patch must make the failing tests pass without breaking others. Verified is a 500-issue subset that human annotators checked.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing scores produced with different harnesses
mistakes.fix: Use the official harness and report settings
Report pass@1 with cost and run time

quiz.question: A vendor says their agent scores 65% on SWE-bench. What do you ask first?
options: Which split (Full, Lite or Verified), with which harness and scaffold, at what cost
Whether the model is open source
quiz.explanation: Scores are only comparable on the same split and set-up, and cost matters too.

quiz.question: A patch fixes the issue but breaks another test. Does it count as resolved?
options: No: the PASS_TO_PASS tests must still pass
Only if the test is flaky
quiz.explanation: Resolved means the issue is fixed and nothing else broke.

quiz.question: What are the limits of public benchmarks? Select all that apply.
options: They do not reflect your domain
quiz.explanation: They are useful for shortlisting, but they do not decide for your use case.

quiz.question: Model B resolves 50% of tasks at $0.10 per attempt. What is its cost per resolved task?
You are shortlisting models for an airline customer-service agent that uses tools and follows policy. Which benchmark fits best?
quiz.explanation: τ-bench simulates customers in retail and airline domains with tools and policies.

quiz.question: Which benchmark fits a browser agent for e-commerce back-office work?
quiz.explanation: WebArena hosts realistic websites, including shopping and admin sites.

quiz.question: The public scoreboard favours Model X, but your own 60 internal issues favour Model Y. Which do you choose?
options: Y, if the internal set reflects your real work
quiz.explanation: Your own tasks predict your results better.

quiz.question: What should you report alongside a benchmark score? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Without these, scores cannot be compared fairly.

quiz.question: Why use the official harness?
Before building a tool-heavy trading assistant, you want to shortlist models on function-call accuracy. Which benchmark fits?
You are automating desktop back-office tasks across real apps. Which benchmark fits?
quiz.explanation: OSWorld tests agents operating real desktop applications.

quiz.question: Your research assistant browses the web, reads files and reasons over many steps. Which benchmark fits?
quiz.explanation: GAIA targets general assistants with browsing, files and multi-step reasoning.

quiz.question: A model scores 20 points higher on an old benchmark than on a similar one released after its training cutoff. What is the likely cause?
options: Contamination: old items may have been in its training data
quiz.explanation: Test items that appear in training data inflate scores.

quiz.question: The top 10 models are all within 1.5 points of each other on a benchmark. What does that mean?
options: The benchmark is saturated and no longer separates models
All models are equal for your use
quiz.explanation: Use harder or private evals to tell the models apart.

quiz.question: 10,000 tasks a month. Model A resolves 60% at $0.30 per attempt; Model B resolves 50% at $0.10. Unresolved tasks go to people at $2 each. Which is cheaper per month?
quiz.explanation: A: $3,000 + 4,000 × $2 = $11,000. B: $1,000 + 5,000 × $2 = $11,000. Include the human fallback in the cost.

quiz.question: A model scores pass^1 = 0.61 and pass^8 = 0.25 on τ-bench retail. What does that tell you?
options: Many tasks succeed only some of the time, so reliability drops sharply over repeated tries
quiz.explanation: τ-bench introduced pass^k to expose exactly this inconsistency.

quiz.question: You are building a private benchmark from your own repositories. What should you do? Select all that apply.
options: Hold back a set you never tune prompts on
Include tests that decide pass or fail
quiz.explanation: Keep it real, held out and automatically checkable.

quiz.question: The same model scores 33% with your in-house agent and 49% on the public board. What is the likely reason?
options: Differences in scaffold and harness: public entries use tuned agent set-ups
quiz.explanation: A score belongs to the whole system, not just the model.

quiz.question: Running your 500-issue suite nightly is getting expensive. What is the best move?
options: Use batch processing and run a small smoke subset on each change
quiz.explanation: Batch APIs cost about half, and a smoke subset keeps quick feedback on each change.

quiz.question: Your team wants to claim “we beat Model X on SWE-bench”. What makes the claim fair? Select all that apply.
options: The same split and the official harness
Stating attempts per issue (pass@1 or best of n)
Quietly picking the best of five runs
quiz.explanation: Be transparent about attempts and set-up. Silent cherry-picking inflates the score.
